Divya-prabandham
(‘divine compositions’)
------------------------------------------
The Viśiṣṭādvaita system of philosophy is also known as ‘Ubhaya Vedānta’, since it recognises two kinds of works (ubhaya = both, two) as equally authoritative. They are: the Sanskrit works commonly known as the ‘prasthānatraya’, viz., the उपनिषद्स्, the Brahmasūtras and the Bhagavadgītā; the Tamil works of the आऌवार्स् known as the Divyaprabandham or Nālāyira Prabandham (since they contain four thousand [nāl = four, āyira = thousand] verses).
The आऌवार्स् were Tamil saints who lived during the period A. D. 700-900. It is their mystical compositions that are known as Divyaprabandham or ‘divine compositions’. An ‘Āḷvār’ is one who is deeply immersed in the love of God. Since these prabandhams or compositions were the spontaneous outpourings of their hearts, deeply immersed in devotional fervour, they are ‘divya’ or divine.
The following is the list of the आऌवार्स् and their compositions:

Since the Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta considers the Divyaprabandham as one of the two cardinal scriptures, the philosophy of the latter is the same as the philosophy of the former. (See VIŚIṢṬĀDVAITA VEDĀNTA DARŚANA.) It can be briefly stated as follows:
The fundamental tattvas or realities are three (tattvatraya). They are ईश्वर (God), cit (the conscious सोउल्) and अचित् (the insentient प्रकृति or nature). ईश्वर is the independent reality whereas the latter two are totally dependent upon him.
The universe is evolved out of the acitprakṛti through 24 cosmic principles (as enumerated in the Sāṅkhya philo-sophy). The cit or the jīva—there are infinite numbers of jīvas—is bound in सṁसार or transmigratory existence since beginning-less time due to कर्म, both good and bad.
It is ईश्वर who out of compassion inspires him to try for मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्. In this attempt for लिबेरतिओन्, the जीव has to rediscover his relationship with ईश्वर, which is of nine kinds: ड़थेर् and son; protector and protected; whole and part; husband and wife; known and knower; master and possession; supporter and supported; सोउल् and body; enjoyer and enjoyed.
The best means of लिबेरतिओन् are: भक्ति (devotion), प्रपत्ति (total surrender to God) and kaiṅkarya (service to God in his various aspects).
The आऌवार्स् seem to be more partial to the path of प्रपत्ति than भक्ति.
The Prabandhas contain profuse praise of the avatāras like राम and कृष्ण, as also the deities in the temples like the ones in श्रीरङ्गम् and तिरुपति, which are known as arcāvatāras and considered as fully living and conscious.
Some of the pāśuras of the praban-dhas are chanted in श्रीवैष्णव temples daily as a part of the worship of the deity.
See also ĀḶVĀRS and ŚRĪVAIṢṆAVISM.

divyaśrotra
(‘divine ear’)
------------------------------------------
The Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि describes the several supernatural powers that a योगि develops by practising सṁयम as directed by it. ‘Saṁyama’ is a technical term signifying धारणा (fixing the मिन्द् on the object of concentration,) ध्यान (continuous meditation on the same) and समाधि (perfect concentration resulting in supernatural or psychic experience) on the same object. By practising सṁयम on the relation between pure आकाश (ether principle, called ‘śabdatanmātra’) and the organ of hearing, both of which being products of अहङ्कार or the cosmic ego-principle, the power to hear sounds, even though they are subtle or at a great distance or separated by other objects, is attained. This is called ‘divyaśrotra’.
The same technique can be applied to other organs too, attaining similar divine powers pertaining to the eye, the nose, the tongue and the skin.
See Yogasūtras 3.41.

divorce
------------------------------------------
Vivāha or मर्रिअगे has been considered as a saṁskāra (a purificatory rite or sacrament). It is one of the three most important of the sixteen सṁस्कारस्, normally called ‘ṣoḍaśasaṁskāras’.
The धर्मशास्त्रस् (religio-legal works) of हिन्दुइस्म् have always considered विवाह as sacred and inviolable. Hence the question of दिवोर्चे or remarriage of widows has not received much attention. Even then, in cases of mutual hatred with the possibility of danger to life and limb, दिवोर्चे has been permitted.
The husband or the wife can abandon the other under certain circumstances such as longstanding incurable disease, becoming ‘patita’ or an outcaste due to heinous sins and so on. Even in such cases bare maintenance has to be provided to the abandoned party.
After the passage of ‘The Hindu मर्रिअगे Act’ in 1955, many desirable changes have been brought about in the system of मर्रिअगे which include provisions for दिवोर्चे also.

divyabhāva
(‘divine disposition’)
------------------------------------------
The tantras—the scriptures of the शक्ति-cult—categorise the sādhakas or spiritual aspirants into three groups according to their bhāvas or dispositions. They are पशु, vīra, and दिव्य.
The sādhakas with the दिव्यभाव are highly sāttvik by nature. They keep themselves meticulously clean, wear clean clothes and the religious marks (tripuṇḍra, भस्म or विभूति), as also the रुद्राक्ष beads. They perform their religious rites like सन्ध्या, जप and पूजा with faith and devotion. They are well-versed in the वेदस् and the scriptures of their cults. They always speak the truth and keep the highest standards of मोरलित्य् and एथिच्स्. They constantly strive for the attainment of devatābhāva or identity with the Divine.
See also TANTRAS.

divyadeśa
(‘divine place’)
------------------------------------------
Milk is got through the udder of a cow, though, theoretically speaking, it pervades the whole body of the cow. Similarly, the तन्त्रस् declare that God, though omnipresent, is found more easily in certain places called ‘divyadeśas’ or divine places. They are enumerated as sixteen in number. Some of them are: vahni (fire), ambu (water), लिङ्ग (Śivaliṅga), मण्डल (specified geometrical diagrams), vigraha (icon or image) and हृदय (the region of the heart).
Dhāraṇā or meditation has to be practised on the इष्टदेवता or chosen deity in these places.

Divodāsa
------------------------------------------
Divodāsa is a common name met with in the Ṛgveda as also in the epics and the पुराणस्.
Divodāsa Atithigva, son of Vadhr-yaśva, was a leading prince among the Bharatas. He was the ड़थेर् (or grand-ड़थेर्) of the famous king सुदास mentioned in the ‘daśarājña’ or the ‘battle of the ten kings’ (vide Ṛgveda 7.33.3 and 5). Śambara, the chieftain of the mountain tribes, was his great enemy.
The son of Bhīmasena, the king of काशी, was also known as दिवोदास. His queen was Mādhavī and प्रतर्दन, his valiant son, who vanquished वीतहव्य, the king of the Haihayas.
This दिवोदास is considered as a reincarnation of धन्वन्तरि, the physician of the gods in हेअवेन्, and the teacher of सुश्रुत (the author of the famous treatise on surgery, the Suśruta Saṁhitā).
Another दिवोदास has been mentioned in the पुराणस् as the son of Bharmyāśva and brother of the famous अहल्या (wife of the sage गौतम).

divyadṛṣṭi
(‘divine sight’)
------------------------------------------
According to the works on योग, clairvoyant powers of perception are inherent in everyone. These powers are roused by appropriate yogic practices.
When saṁyama—dhāraṇā, ध्यान and samādhi—is practised on the पुरुष or the individual सोउल्, the योगि attains special supernatural powers, of which दिव्यदृष्टि or ādarśa is also one (vide Yogasūtras 3.36). He is then able to ‘see’ objects which may be extremely small or hidden by other things or at a great distance or belonging to a past time or a future time.
Such सिद्धिस् or supernatural powers can prove to be obstacles to spiritual illumination.
Lord कृष्ण is said to have given दिव्यदृष्टि to अर्जुन before showing his cosmic form (Bhagavadgītā 11.8).
The sage व्यास gave the power to सञ्जय, to ‘see’ the कुरुक्षेत्र battle from the palace itself (Mahābhārata, Bhīṣmaparva 2.9).
See also SAṀYAMA.

divya
(‘divine’, ‘supernatural’)
------------------------------------------
Though this word generally means ‘divine,’ it is used in the धर्मशास्त्रस् in a more technical sense. When a king had to decide whether a particular person had committed a crime or not, especially when the evidence normally relied upon, like eye-witness accounts or strong circum-stantial evidence, was not conclusive, he could take recourse to ‘divya’ or supernatural mode of evidence. ‘Divya’ is defined as ‘that which decides a matter in dispute, not determined by human means of proof’.
The suspect is subjected to an ordeal and is declared innocent if he comes out unharmed. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (6.16.1) refers to the ordeal of holding a heated axe in hand by a suspected thief. If he is not scalded, he is considered innocent and freed.
Such divyas can range from two to nine. Some of them are: viṣa (administering poison), kośapāna (drinking holy water, used for bathing an image in worship), phāla (licking a red-hot ploughshare), taṇḍula (swallowing rice-grains specially prepared) and taptamāṣa (taking out heated gold pieces with bare fingers).
The details of the tests are described in the dharmaśāstra works.
Physical laws of nature are inexorable. How can they fail in such tests? For this objection the answer given by the writers of the dharamaśāstras is that even the normal processes of strong evidence have sometimes failed to prove the guilt. And, supernatural things, unexplained mysteries, are happening, even now.
